prompt: Human: How do I teach my kids to speak French?
response:
That’s a great question, and it’s one that many parents ask.  I can offer a few suggestions, but first a bit of history:  French was the language of choice for much of Western Europe for about a million years after the arrival of agriculture, so it had a lot of influence on the languages of Europe.  The French language has a rich tradition of written and spoken poetry, and I’ll focus on the written language in this answer.  I’ll also mention the important role of the Académie française in preserving the French language and culture.  As you probably know, France has a very high rate of education for its citizens, and while they take their language seriously, they’re also really good about speaking and writing in English.  Today, French is the second most common language spoken on the Internet, so it’s certainly used in your kids’ daily lives.  So here are some tips:

1.  Start with the basics

Reading, writing, and listening are the three pillars of language learning.  There are many good free online tools for practicing the basics, including Duolingo, Lingodeer, ABCmouse, and Babbel.  I like the free app Duolingo, because it teaches grammar and vocabulary in a way that feels really natural, and because you’re free to switch back and forth between English and French.  Duolingo can also be helpful if you want to learn other languages, and there are additional tools there that can help you with conversational practice.
2.  Be patient and persistent

French is a beautiful language, and mastering it will take time.  At the same time, you’ll probably find that it’s really easy to learn from reading and writing, and the more familiar it is, the easier it will be to talk and to hear people speaking.  Learning will be especially frustrating, but it’s also one of the best parts.  I remember being really frustrated the first time I tried to read, but then I remembered that one of my French teachers told me to just keep trying, and it really paid off.
3.  Listen to a lot of French

France used to be a dominant global power, and it continues to be a great place to live and work.  In recent years, France has seen a decline in its global influence, but in all likelihood you’ll find French on the radio, TV, and your online world, so listening is a great way to start.  There are many internet radio and video websites that offer French content that should be accessible to anyone.  The French TV channel, France 2, has a great public schedule of when their shows and movies are coming up.
4.  Write your own French stories and poetry

This is a really cool way to learn, because it feels like you’re really taking your own words into your own hands.  You’ll also be working on a skill that will help you in many other aspects of your life.  Try writing a story, an essay, or a poem in French, and check it out for feedback.  I’ve seen many children using the book “Little Bear” as a model for writing stories, but you could also try writing your own.  Here’s a short story I came up with in French.  It has some good advice for a young child, and it’s also a bit of a challenge in French.  If you end up trying to translate it, keep in mind that there are many different ways to write the same thing.  You could make it rhyme, you could switch from the present tense to the past.  There are many ways to express what this sentence means.  Do your best to figure out what works the best in the language of your choice.
5.  Learn a little history of France

Learning the details of a country’s history is always helpful, and even if you’re just starting out with French, it can still be really interesting to learn about France’s past.  It can help if you learn some of the French phrases like “le roi” and “le pays” and know what they mean, and it’ll also help if you learn a little about the French Revolution, a period in French history that had a huge impact on France and the world.  If you’ve got time, I recommend reading a little about it in English, so you’ll be familiar with some of the concepts it will bring up.  Here are some good articles to start with. 
6.  Find people who speak French

This is a good one, if you want to practice speaking and listening to French, you’ll probably want to find people who speak it.  I recommend finding a language exchange buddy on Skype.  I’ve found that having a friend who can speak your native language is really helpful, but it can be a little tricky to find people through language exchange apps, so if you can’t find one, you might have to do it manually.  You could also ask friends and acquaintances if they would like to have a language exchange, but keep in mind that they’ll probably be hesitant to talk to you if they know you can’t speak French well.  Try asking people around your area if they’d be interested in a conversation.  If you really want to practice speaking, you could try recording a conversation, but if you want to really get the most out of it, I recommend going to a café, coffee shop, or even your own bedroom and having a real conversation.  This is something that will be helpful in many different contexts.
7.  Take a course

Many online tools will recommend taking a French course, and that’s definitely a good idea, but if you don’t want to do just one class, it might be better to find a person to teach you how to learn French well.  In my opinion, it’s the best way to learn French if you want to become fluent and speak it well at an advanced level.  It will also be more interesting and take more time.  When I took classes with a French teacher, she could give me feedback on my writing and grammar, and we could have longer conversations in French.  If you find a teacher online, you’ll probably want to find one in the UK or France.  My experience is that the UK is probably the most reasonable, but it’s worth checking out the availability of classes in France as well.  If you want just one short class, you can also take a one-to-one or a short weekend course.  It may be worth checking out whether these options are available in your local area.  I recommend looking at their websites and reading a little about their experience.  I know from personal experience that one-on-one classes can really help with speaking, and I learned a lot about how to approach conversation with French speakers in those classes.  If you have a large amount of money to spend on language classes, you might want to look at Skype or FaceTime classes, which are good when you have a large group of people.  I can recommend some good programs for Skype and FaceTime classes.  I remember spending hours on FaceTime classes with an experienced French teacher.  Many of the teachers on these programs have great experiences, and they will probably be more willing to help if you ask for some feedback from them after you’ve taken a class with them.

Ingredients:

8 oz. or 220 g. firm or extra-firm Israeli cheese (Eghobalanuʼa or Kosharyouna)

1 small red onion, finely chopped

1 clove garlic, minced

1 tsp. fresh lemon juice

2 tbsp. olive oil

Kosher salt and pepper

1/4 cup chopped fresh parsley

1 lemon, sliced (optional)

4.  Bake for 10-15 minutes, or until the cheese is melted and bubbly.
